science.title: Agreement among large language models does not track medical truth in health claim verification
science.description: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as tools to verify online health information. A common assumption from the self-consistency and ensemble literature is that agreement across models signals reliability. But it remains untested whether inter-model consensus tracks medical truth. We evaluated 10 LLMs spanning frontier, Russian-specific and medical-specialized families on RuHealth, a corpus of 108 short health claims (40 true, 40 false, 28 disputed) validated through multi-stage physician review. Each claim was classified as true, false, or disputed, in both Russian and a validated English translation, across decoding temperatures and 3 stochastic runs ($${\sim }$$90,000 judgements). Frontier models were most accurate (macro-F1 64–70) but no model was reliable: “disputed” was assigned to 59.8% of judgements versus a 26% true base rate, while false claims were systematically missed. Majority voting did not help. Three frontier models were unanimous on 90 of 108 claims, yet 31% of those unanimous verdicts were wrong, and 26 of 28 assigned “disputed” to claims that were actually true (14) or false (12). Thus, in this setting on health claims, agreement among contemporary LLMs is not evidence of medical correctness; this effect, which we term consensus mirage, proves to be robust to prompt wording and language.

science.title: APH-Net: a multi-task uncertainty-weighted neural architecture for subgroup-level pediatric health surveillance modeling
science.description: Aggregated public health tables contain repeated demographic and temporal estimates, but random record-level splits can overstate predictive performance when the same subgroup definitions occur in both training and test data. This study evaluates APH-Net, a condition-conditioned multi-task neural architecture, using a CDC surveillance table with 1,203 condition-stratum-period cells across eight health conditions, 25 marginal subgroup strata, and seven reporting windows. The primary evaluation withheld five complete subgroup strata (197 cells), while model selection used only the remaining 1,006 cells. XGBoost achieved the strongest primary regression performance (MAE = 1.272, RMSE = 1.699, R² = 0.862; 95% CI 0.823–0.887 for R²), followed by APH-Net (R² = 0.853) and Random Forest (R² = 0.838). For the auxiliary above-training-median classification task, XGBoost achieved ROC-AUC = 0.775 and macro-F1 = 0.626, whereas APH-Net achieved ROC-AUC = 0.627. Repeated subgroup holdouts and a non-overlapping temporal test produced lower and more variable performance than random-split estimates. APH-Net ablation showed task-dependent value: classification discrimination improved over a single-head MLP, while regression did not. The findings support subgroup-level surveillance modeling but not individual clinical risk prediction.
